study.title: Proverbs 31 - wisdom to rule and to live with fear of the Lord
study.overview: Proverbs 31 brings together two complementary instructions. In verses 1-9, a mother guides a king over self-control, justice, and defense of the vulnerable. In verses 1031, the book concludes with a poem that exalts the virtuous woman, describing her diligence, prudence, generosity, wisdom, and fear of the Lord. The chapter concludes by showing that true value is not in appearance, but in the character approved by God and publicly recognized.

outline.title: Mother's Advice to a King
outline.explanation: The initial speech presents words taught by Lemuel's mother. The focus is on the fair government: avoiding desires that weaken, not surrender to drink, protect the right of the weak and speak for those who cannot defend themselves.

outline.title: Portrait of the virtuous woman
outline.explanation: The poem describes a wife and exemplary administrator: reliable, hardworking, foresightful, generous, wise in speaking and attentive to the house. Its activity reaches home, trade and care for those in need.

outline.title: End Praise to the Lord's Fear
outline.explanation: The family praises it, but the text states that the foundation of his dignity is the fear of the Lord. Beauty passes; the godly character remains and must be publicly recognized.

study.context: The notes indicate that Lemuel is a little-known king outside of this passage. Tyndale notes that his mother instructs him to control desires and alcohol to reign with justice. It is also noted that the poem of the virtuous woman is presented as an organized composition in alphabetical form, which suggests completeness and facilitates memorization. References to the elders at the city's doorpoint the public environment of community trial and deliberation in Israel.
study.theology: The chapter unites government and domestic life under the same principle: the fear of the Lord. The king needs to dominate appetites not to corrupt justice; the virtuous woman expresses wisdom in concrete actions, service, prudence and generosity. Thus, Proverbs 31 teaches that biblical spirituality is not abstract: it appears in the way it governs itself, works, administers the house, speaks and is the needy. The text also corrects superficial values, remembering that physical beauty is transient, while the faithful character to God deserves lasting praise. In evangelical reading, this is not a generic exaltation of human effort, but a vision of wisdom shaped by reverence to the Lord and confirmed by visible fruits.

scholarViews.insight: The exhortation of Lemuel's mother aims to restrain her desires, especially for women and drink, so that he may reign with justice.
The chapter is presented as inspired and organized prophecy in two parts: the warning to the young prince and the description of the virtuous woman.
The chapter contrasts the depravity and excess of wine with the king's righteous administration, and then passes to the praise of the virtuous and diligent woman.

questions: What habits or desires can compromise my ability to act with justice and discernment?
What concrete attitudes of this poem describe a wise life in the home, work and relationship with others?
Instead of seeking only appearance or public image, how can I cultivate the fear of the Lord who sustains a character approved by God?
study.practice: Choose an area where you need more self-control, fairness or practical diligence. Pray for this and adopt a concrete attitude this week: limit something that weakens you, defend someone who needs a voice, or serve your home with more attention and wisdom. It is also worth reading the chapter as a mirror: ask what traces of the text already appear in your life and which need regret and growth.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes do not allow us to safely identify who Lemuel was or confirm historical details beyond what the commentators suggest. The connection of the virtuous woman's poem with a specific authorship or with a precise date cannot be treated as a certain fact from these sources. Some expressions of the translated biblical text are difficult and therefore certain images can admit more than one interpretive nuance.
